records.term: Assembly of the wicked / synagogue of Satan
records.definition: A counterfeit congregation claiming covenant standing while gathered against the covenant's Lord. Korah's company; the brood of vipers and children of the Devil, the father of lies; the assembly surrounding the Messiah; and those who say they are Jews but are not display the pattern.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A community that claims religious legitimacy or covenant identity but, through opposition to God, Christ, or faithful believers, functions as an instrument of Satan. In Christian interpretation, the expression usually signifies false or hostile religion rather than a building or an assembly openly dedicated to Satan.
judges.strongestObjection: The entry may compress historically distinct groups and texts into one canonical type, and the printed excerpts alone do not establish every lexical nuance of “edah” or the inside/outside-camp distinction. Nevertheless, Numbers explicitly depicts an allegedly holy congregation gathered against God’s appointed leaders, Psalms depicts wicked assemblies, Acts identifies those gathered against Jesus, and Revelation names false covenant claimants the synagogue of Satan.
judges.materialContradiction: None. The book neither replaces the consensus referent nor denies its historical or theological applications.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the phrase denotes a counterfeit covenant community: a group that claims the identity and privileges of God's people while in fact opposing God and persecuting the faithful, thereby serving Satan rather than God. In its original setting in Revelation, the dominant historical-critical reading takes it as the local Jewish synagogue communities in Smyrna and Philadelphia who denounced or slandered Christians to Roman authorities; the theological point drawn from it in Christian interpretation is that outward religious identity without allegiance to Christ is a false claim, so that the 'assembly' stands symbolically for false or apostate religion in opposition to the true people of God. The related phrase 'assembly of the wicked' (Psalm 22:16) is traditionally read christologically as the hostile crowd surrounding the suffering righteous one, applied in Christian exegesis to those who condemned and crucified Christ.
judges.strongestObjection: One could argue MATCH: the consensus already recognizes 'assembly of the wicked'/'synagogue of Satan' as false covenant claimants opposing God, and the OT verses merely illustrate the same idea rather than materially extending it; Response A even notes the synagoge/assembly linguistic linkage. On that view the Numbers typology and inside/outside reading are elaboration, not boundary change. However, treating the wilderness congregation and Korah's company as instances of the term itself — and splitting Psalm 22:16 into insider/outsider persecutors — goes beyond what any consensus response asserts, so REFINED is the better fit.
judges.materialContradiction: None. The book affirms the consensus core — false covenant claimants gathered against God — and its Revelation reading ('say they are Jews, and are not') is fully compatible with all consensus responses. The added OT typology enriches rather than replaces the referent.

The book identifies the term as the counterfeit congregation — an 'edah' (the covenant-assembly word) claiming covenant standing while gathered against the covenant's Lord. It traces a typological pattern: the wilderness generation named 'this evil congregation gathered together against me' (Num 14:35), Korah's company declaring the whole congregation holy while rebelling (Num 16:3), and at the cross the 'assembly of the wicked' enclosing the Messiah from inside the camp (Israel, per Acts 4:27) while the 'dogs' compass from without (Gentiles), culminating in Revelation's 'synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not.'

It further reclassifies the elements of Ps 22:16 (dogs = outsiders, assembly = insiders), a distinction absent from consensus. records.definition: The firstfruits grain — humble, reaped in spring, and presented before the LORD. Its waved sheaf points to Christ risen as the firstfruits.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Barley has no universally settled Christian symbolic meaning. Where a broad symbolism is assigned, it most often represents humble or inexpensive sustenance through which God provides—especially provision for ordinary or poor people.
judges.strongestObjection: The cited texts establish that barley ripens early, can be called firstfruits, and that Paul calls the risen Christ 'the firstfruits,' but no cited verse explicitly identifies the Levitical sheaf as barley or directly states that barley symbolizes Christ. The final equivalence therefore depends on typological synthesis.
judges.materialContradiction: None. The book’s identification is explicitly represented in every consensus response, either as the primary meaning or as a recognized alternative.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In most Christian teaching, barley symbolizes humble, lowly provision — the bread of the poor — through which God works and provides. Because barley was the cheaper grain eaten by the poor (about half the value of wheat), it is read as a picture of humility, lowliness, and God's use of small or despised means, most famously in the boy's five barley loaves with which Jesus feeds the five thousand. Closely intertwined with this is a second widely taught meaning: barley as the firstfruits grain of the early (Passover-season) harvest, and therefore a type of resurrection and of the 'firstfruits' people of God.
judges.strongestObjection: One could argue REFINED on grounds that the book elevates the firstfruits/Christ-risen typology to definitional status while much academic commentary treats barley non-symbolically, and that 'humblest' is not directly evidenced by the printed verses. But the consensus explicitly lists firstfruits/resurrection as a common-to-primary reading, so no boundary or extension actually shifts; also Lev 23:10 does not name barley, requiring the Ex 9:31 inference, which slightly weakens the printed-citation chain.
judges.materialContradiction: None. The book's identification is an explicit combination of the two most prominent consensus meanings.

judgmentRationales: The entry is not novel: the blind responses already identify heaven with divine rule, the physical sky, and the renewed union of heaven and earth. Nor is it a match, because the book combines these senses into a jurisdictional definition and excludes the common final-destination framing. Since it preserves the central referent of God's sphere of authority while materially revising which senses and eschatological cases belong under it, the relationship is refined.

The book's central referent is still the consensus referent — the realm of God's presence, throne, and rule (Isa 66:1 cited by both). So the core is not replaced. But the book materially tightens the boundary: it rejects the consensus's derivative identification of heaven as the place the redeemed go up to, replacing it with a descent-only eschatology. This move is anticipated in the consensus itself: Responses A and C explicitly list the new-heavens-and-new-earth / New-Jerusalem-descends view (N. T. Wright-style) as a common alternative, so the book's position is a sharpened selection within the recognized field, not a novel or contradictory identification. Its distinctive 'jurisdiction of accomplished will' and anti-Babel framing adds precision and polemical edge rather than a new referent. bookSummaries: The book identifies “life” as covenant existence produced by obedience to the law.

The book defines 'life' as covenant existence — the life that the law produces — grounding this in Deut 30:19-20 and Lev 18:5 ('if a man do [my statutes], he shall live in them'), and applying this legal-covenantal reading even to John 14:6 and Matt 7:14. judgmentRationales: The book’s reading is not novel because covenant flourishing, righteous life, and life associated with obedience were expressly recognized in the consensus alternatives. Nevertheless, the consensus treats that as a contextual or secondary usage, whereas the book makes law-produced covenant existence the core meaning, including for John 14:6. This replaces the consensus’s central Christological referent and therefore is divergent rather than refined.

The book's core identification replaces, rather than sharpens, the consensus core. Response B lists 'covenant flourishing through fidelity to God' as a common alternative for OT usage, so the raw idea is not absent from the consensus space; but the book elevates that secondary register into the primary meaning and applies it to the very Johannine texts (John 14:6) that anchor the consensus christological/eternal-life reading, while explicitly marking the common teaching as what it departs from. That is replacement of the central referent with partial reclassification of shared cases, which fits DIVERGENT rather than REFINED (the consensus's central referent does not remain intact) or NOVEL (the covenant-law reading appears among listed alternatives).

Minimum cores are non-equivalent: consensus primary is the person/gift of Christ as divine life; book primary is the product of law-keeping. Alternatives list covenant flourishing (e.g., Deut 30), so the book is not wholly unattested, yet presenting that as the entry (while noting the Christ view as common) requires replacing rather than refining or overlapping the consensus core. Extension therefore concerns a different referent, not a subset/superset of the same cases. Citations mix OT law-life texts with Christ-as-life texts, confirming the divergence rather than resolving it.

bookSummaries: Light is God’s law embodied in publicly visible righteous conduct—good works that others can see.

The book defines light as 'the law lived visibly — good works others can see,' fusing Proverbs 6:23 (the law is light) with Matthew 5:16 (let your light shine through visible good works). Light is thus embodied obedience to God's law made publicly observable, rather than God or Christ as the divine referent; a fuller treatment is deferred to a 'Light and Darkness' chapter.

judgmentRationales: The book does not introduce an unknown referent or replace the consensus with an incompatible one. Proverbs 6:23 explicitly associates law with light, while Matthew 5:16 links shining light with publicly seen good works. The book synthesizes these established strands into a materially narrower identification rather than preserving the full polyvalent consensus.

The book's core is not absent from consensus (so not NOVEL) and does not assert something that cannot be true alongside the consensus's polyvalent readings (so not DIVERGENT in the strict contradictory sense): the consensus itself lists both 'God's word/law as light' and 'believers' visible righteous conduct' as common recognized meanings. However, the book materially relocates the symbol's center from the divine referent to human obedience-made-visible, redrawing the boundary of what 'light' properly denotes. That is a real boundary disagreement — a narrowing and re-centering onto derivative senses — rather than mere rewording, so REFINED with BOOK_NARROWS/BOOK_SUBSET is the accurate classification. The cross-reference to a 'Light and Darkness' chapter suggests the divine sense may be handled elsewhere, further indicating deliberate narrowing rather than replacement.

judgmentRationales: God’s law is not novel: all three consensus responses include God’s word or Scripture, and several cite Psalm 119’s identification of the law with truth. The overlap in scriptural cases therefore does not remove the referential divergence.

Although 'Scripture/God's word' appears among consensus alternatives, the book does not merely narrow that alternative — it elevates 'God's law' to the exclusive primary identification while displacing the Christocentric center that every blind response names as the dominant referent. The book's explicit framing ('Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and God's word — the gospel that sets free') confirms it intends a different referent, not a refinement. Because the central referent is replaced (law-as-standard instead of Christ-in-person/gospel), while some extensional cases (Psalm 119; Johannine 'walking in truth') are retained, this is DIVERGENT with partial reclassification rather than REFINED.

Minimum cores are non-equivalent: consensus responses A/B/C all fix Christ (via John 14:6 and related Johannine texts) as the settled primary while listing law/word only among alternatives; the book instead installs God's law as the entry itself and explicitly flags the Christ/gospel reading as the common view. This is referent replacement, not a boundary adjustment around a shared category.

bookSummaries: Works are deeds, but not inherently obedience. A deed counts as obedience or disobedience according to its relation to a legitimate divine command; even complete obedience remains duty rather than wage-earning merit.

The book identifies works simply as deeds, but insists that 'works' is not a synonym for obedience: a work only becomes obedience when it executes a legitimate command, and becomes disobedience when it conflicts with God's command. It further holds that even complete obedience earns no wage (the unprofitable-servant principle of Luke 17), reading Romans 4 as wage/debt vocabulary and James 2 as Abraham's work making faith visible. It rejects the common teaching that Paul's 'works' broadly bundles human obedience and effort as a category set against faith.

Works are simply deeds, not a synonym for obedience. A work becomes obedience only when it executes a legitimate command (or disobedience when it conflicts with God's command). Romans 4 treats the laborer's work as offered for wages/debt; James 2 treats Abraham's work as faith made visible. Even complete obedience earns no wage, since the servant has only done his duty.
judgmentRationales: Both readings identify works centrally as deeds. The book does not replace that referent, but adds a governing distinction: deeds become obedience only by executing legitimate commands and can instead constitute disobedience. It also sharpens the works–wages distinction by combining Romans 4 with Luke 17. Because these conditions materially revise how cases are classified without changing the central category, the relationship is REFINED rather than MATCH or DIVERGENT.

The book preserves the consensus's central referent — works are deeds — so DIVERGENT is inappropriate. But the disagreement is more than wording: it materially changes the conceptual structure by denying the works-obedience synonymy that runs through the consensus responses and the common-view note, by making obedience a conditional status of a work relative to a command, and by asserting that even complete obedience earns nothing (undercutting both the merit alternative and the loose 'obedience and effort vs. faith' framing of Paul). This is real boundary and classification disagreement within the same category, which fits REFINED. It is not NOVEL because the deed-referent and the faith-made-visible reading of James 2 are squarely within consensus territory.

Minimum cores both reduce to 'deeds/actions.' The book preserves that general category and the Rom 4 / Jas 2 usages while materially tightening boundaries and conditions: it rejects synonymy with obedience, reclassifies when a deed counts as obedience vs. mere work, and foregrounds the Luke 17 duty/no-wage principle. This is refinement of extension and precision, not replacement of the central referent or a novel category outside the consensus.

objections.text: The printed texts strongly support the denial that works of the law justify or produce the Spirit, but they do not by themselves establish that the phrase lacks a stable Torah-observance referent. Galatians 3:10’s appeal to doing everything written in the law may instead suggest that actual Torah performance remains integral to the phrase’s meaning.

One could argue MATCH: all three responses already deny settled consensus and list multiple scope options, and the book's 'context decides' move merely restates that interpretive plurality rather than materially disagreeing with any consensus claim; the shared theological core (works of the law cannot justify) is identical.

The cited Pauline texts occur in tightly related Mosaic-law or Jewish-practice contexts, so the book's denial of any unchanging class may overstate variability and underplay textual consistency of the referent.

contradictions.text: The NPP counter denies the book's core by asserting that the phrase does identify one unchanging class of deeds — the ethnic boundary markers — in every occurrence, and that Paul's target is exclusivism rather than the deed's claimed purchase-power; both cannot be true of the same phrase, since the book explicitly classifies Romans 3:20, 28 and Galatians 3:10 as God's law generally, not badges.

unresolvedObjections.text: The evidence does not establish that erga nomou itself lexically expresses a purchase-price claim; that force may arise from Paul’s surrounding contrasts and predicates.
The supplied occurrences can all plausibly remain within the broad category of Mosaic Torah observance, so the assertion that no stable class is identified is insufficiently demonstrated.
The book’s distinction between “God’s law,” a “circumcision-party application,” and unnamed acts may classify contextual emphasis rather than genuinely different referents.
Several extended conclusions about continuing Torah application go beyond what is necessary to identify “works of the law” and are more contestable than the accepted core.

A defensible middle reading holds that erga nomou has a constant surface referent (deeds of the Mosaic Torah) applied in varied controversies, so the 'no unchanging class' claim may overstate the variation; Gal 2:16 arguably still means Torah-deeds even though the circumcision party is the occasion.
The Galatians 3:2, 5 classification as 'ambiguous/unnamed acts' is debatable, since the letter's live controversy (circumcision) plausibly names the act implicitly.
The Romans 9:32 entry depends on the KJV/TR reading; on the critical text that verse drops out of the phrase's occurrence list entirely.
The book does not engage 4QMMT, the strongest extrabiblical datum the sectarian-halakhah and NPP readings cite, so the phrase's Second Temple usage remains unaddressed.
Some readers may still prefer a narrower New-Perspective restriction to boundary markers alone, even though that restriction fails for the explicit 'book of the law' citations
The precise relationship between the rejected purchase-price claim and later Spirit-enabled obedience remains a matter of systematic theology beyond the lexical scope of the entry

bookSummaries: The book treats the phrase as context-dependent deeds considered in relation to law, not as a fixed class or a synonym for obedience. Its constant element is the invalid claim that such deeds can purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or put God in debt.

The phrase is Paul's designation for deeds considered in relation to law, with no single unchanging class of deeds as its referent: context may identify God's law, a circumcision-party application, or leave the acts unnamed. What is constant is not the deeds but the rejected claim made for them—that they can purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt. The phrase functions as a denial of the deeds as purchase price, not as a fixed category label.

Paul's phrase for deeds considered in relation to law; it is not a synonym for obedience and does not name one unchanging class of deeds. Context may identify God's law, a circumcision-party application, or leave the acts unnamed, but what is constant is denial that the deeds can purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt.
judgmentRationales: This is REFINED rather than MATCH because the book materially changes how cases are classified: “works of the law” is not a fixed set of Mosaic-law observances but a contextual category unified by an invalid instrumental claim. It is not DIVERGENT because it retains the consensus’s central law-related referent and justification contrast, and the consensus itself already contains alternatives involving boundary markers and particular halakhic applications.

The book retains the consensus's general category—law-related deeds Paul denies as the basis of justification—and retains the functional theological point on which all consensus readings agree (these works cannot justify). So the core is not replaced; there is compatible overlap. But the book materially changes the precision and extension: instead of adjudicating among fixed-referent options, it reclassifies the phrase as having a variable, context-supplied referent unified only by the denied transactional claim. This reclassifies cases across the consensus alternatives (each becomes locally correct rather than definitionally correct) and rejects the shared assumption of a single unchanging class, including the equation with 'obedience.' That is a real boundary-level disagreement without contradiction of the central referent, which fits REFINED. Response B's note that the scope may be 'some combination' gestures toward this, but no consensus response articulates the book's context-relative, claim-centered account as its primary meaning.

Minimum cores both identify the phrase with law-related deeds whose power to justify (or produce the Spirit/standing) is denied. The book preserves that general category and the key Pauline rejection but materially refines precision and boundaries by rejecting synonymy with obedience or a fixed deed-class, making extension context-variable (covering circumcision-party cases among others). This is boundary/extension disagreement, not core replacement.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'year' most commonly carries the symbolic sense of a complete, divinely appointed period of time — above all 'the acceptable year of the Lord,' i.e., the era of God's favor, salvation, and release. This draws on the Jubilee year (a fiftieth-year proclamation of liberty, debt release, and restoration) as a type of messianic redemption, which Jesus applies to his own ministry in the Nazareth synagogue. Thus 'year' symbolizes the full season or epoch of God's saving activity rather than a mere calendar unit.
